(CNN) -- Massachusetts sued the U.S. government on Wednesday, challenging the constitutionality of a federal law that defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman. The state of Massachusetts says the Defense of Marriage Act denies same-sex couples essential rights. "We're taking this action today because, first, we believe that [the Defense of Marriage Act] directly interferes with Massachusetts' long-standing sovereign authority to define and regulate the marital status of its residents," Attorney General Martha Coakley said Wednesday afternoon. "Massachusetts has a single category of married persons, and we view all married persons equally and identically," she said. "DOMA divides that category into two distinct and unequal classes of marriage." The lawsuit argues that the act, which became law in 1996, denies same-sex couples essential rights and protections, including federal income tax credits, employment and retirement benefits, health insurance coverage and Social Security payments. "In enacting DOMA, Congress overstepped its authority, undermined states' efforts to recognize marriages between same-sex couples, and codified an animus towards gay and lesbian people," the state wrote in the lawsuit, which was filed Wednesday in federal court. Massachusetts, the first state to legalize gay marriage, said that about 16,000 same-sex couples have been married there since 2004, when it began issuing marriage licenses. Since that time, the lawsuit said, "the security and stability of families has been strengthened in important ways throughout the state. " The state is challenging Section 3 of the law, which defines marriage as "a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife" and a spouse as "a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife." Before the act, the lawsuit argues, defining marital status was the prerogative of the states. The law "eviscerated more than 200 years of federal government deference to the states with respect to defining marriage," it said. The lawsuit also argues that the law forces Massachusetts to treat same-sex married couples differently from heterosexual married couples, particularly through determining who qualifies for the state's Medicaid program, known as MassHealth, and whether a same-sex spouse of a veteran can be buried in a veteran cemetery. "But for DOMA, married individuals in same-sex relationships in the commonwealth would receive the same status, obligations, responsibilities, rights, and protections as married individuals in different-sex relationships under local, state, and federal laws," the lawsuit said. The defendants named in the lawsuit include the Department of Health and Human Services, Secretary of Health and Human Services Kathleen Sebelius, the Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki and the United States itself. Charles Miller, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, said the department will review the case but noted that President Obama supports the legislative repeal of the Defense of Marriage Act. In March, Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders -- the same Boston-based group that successfully argued in 2003 for same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts -- also sued the federal government over Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act. Besides Massachusetts, three other states recognize same-sex marriages: Connecticut, Maine, and Iowa. Vermont and New Hampshire will join their company when same-sex marriages become legal later this year and early next year.

(CNN) — On Wednesday, Massachusetts filed a lawsuit against the federal government, arguing that a federal statute defining marriage solely as a union between one man and one woman is unconstitutional.

State officials contend that the Defense of Marriage Act, known as DOMA, deprives same-sex couples of important legal rights.

Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley said Wednesday afternoon that the state was bringing the case because DOMA “directly interferes” with Massachusetts’ established authority to determine and regulate the marital status of people living in the state.

Coakley said Massachusetts recognizes only one class of married people and treats every married person the same. DOMA, she said, separates that single group into “two distinct and unequal classes of marriage.”

The complaint says the 1996 law withholds key rights and protections from married same-sex couples, including federal income tax credits, job-related and retirement benefits, health coverage, and Social Security payments.

In the lawsuit, filed Wednesday in federal court, Massachusetts argued that Congress exceeded its constitutional power by passing DOMA, weakened state efforts to recognize same-sex marriages, and wrote hostility toward gay and lesbian people into federal law.

Massachusetts, which was the first state to permit gay marriage, said roughly 16,000 same-sex couples have married there since the state began granting marriage licenses in 2004. Since then, the lawsuit said, families across Massachusetts have gained greater security and stability in significant ways.

The state’s challenge focuses on Section 3 of DOMA. That section defines marriage as “a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife” and defines a spouse as “a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife.”

According to the lawsuit, before DOMA was enacted, the power to define marital status belonged to the states. The complaint says the law wiped away more than two centuries of federal deference to state authority over marriage definitions.

Massachusetts also claims DOMA compels the state to treat married same-sex couples differently from married heterosexual couples. The lawsuit points in particular to decisions about eligibility for the state Medicaid program, MassHealth, and whether the same-sex spouse of a veteran may be buried in a veterans cemetery.

The complaint states that without DOMA, married people in same-sex relationships in Massachusetts would have the same legal status, duties, responsibilities, rights, and protections as married people in opposite-sex relationships under local, state, and federal law.

The lawsuit names several defendants, including the Department of Health and Human Services, Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius, the Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki, and the United States government.

Charles Miller, a Justice Department spokesman, said the department would examine the lawsuit. He also noted that President Obama supports repealing the Defense of Marriage Act through legislation.

In March, Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders, the Boston organization that successfully argued the 2003 case establishing same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts, also brought a federal lawsuit challenging Section 3 of DOMA.

In addition to Massachusetts, three states recognize same-sex marriages: Connecticut, Maine, and Iowa. Vermont and New Hampshire are set to join them when same-sex marriage becomes legal there later this year and early next year.

*Original news-style summary based on 2009 events*

**BOSTON, Massachusetts —** Massachusetts officials filed a constitutional challenge Wednesday to a key section of the federal Defense of Marriage Act, arguing that the law unlawfully denies federal recognition to same-sex marriages that are legal under state law.

The lawsuit, brought by Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley, targets **Section 3 of DOMA**, the 1996 federal law that defines marriage, for federal purposes, as the union of one man and one woman. Coakley said the law interferes with the state’s authority to define and regulate marriage, an area traditionally controlled by states. The complaint argues that DOMA forces Massachusetts to discriminate against its own married citizens in the administration of federally funded programs and denies the state and its residents equal treatment.

The lawsuit claims that Section 3 of DOMA exceeds Congress’ authority and violates constitutional principles by penalizing Massachusetts for recognizing marriages that are valid under state law. It also argues the law imposes administrative burdens on the state because Massachusetts must treat same-sex married couples differently when handling certain federal programs.

The Justice Department, which is responsible for defending federal statutes in court, said the administration would review the complaint. President Obama has said he supports repeal of DOMA, but the administration has also stated that the Justice Department generally has a duty to defend laws passed by Congress unless there is no reasonable argument in their favor.

The filing came amid growing national debate over same-sex marriage. In 2009, a handful of states allowed same-sex couples to marry, while others had constitutional amendments or statutes defining marriage as between a man and a woman.

Supporters of the Massachusetts lawsuit said DOMA unfairly denies married same-sex couples access to federal protections available to other married couples. Opponents of same-sex marriage argued that Congress acted within its authority when it enacted DOMA and that federal law should not be required to recognize same-sex marriages from individual states.

The case marked one of the most direct state challenges to DOMA since the law was signed by President Bill Clinton in 1996.

Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley filed a lawsuit against the federal government challenging the Defense of Marriage Act, known as DOMA, arguing that the law unlawfully discriminated against legally married same-sex couples and interfered with Massachusetts’ authority to define and regulate marriage.

DOMA, enacted in 1996, allowed the federal government to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages even if those marriages were valid under state law. Massachusetts had legalized same-sex marriage in 2004, but because of DOMA, couples married in Massachusetts were still treated as unmarried for many federal purposes.

Coakley’s lawsuit argued that this created a two-tier system: Massachusetts recognized same-sex spouses as married, while the federal government denied them the rights, benefits, and responsibilities available to other married couples. The state also contended that DOMA forced Massachusetts to discriminate against its own citizens in order to comply with federal programs.

Key areas affected included:

- **Federal taxes:** Married same-sex couples could not file joint federal tax returns, even though they were married under Massachusetts law. This often led to higher tax burdens and complicated filings, because couples had to file as married for state taxes but as single individuals for federal taxes.

- **Social Security benefits:** Surviving same-sex spouses were denied federal spousal and survivor benefits available to opposite-sex spouses. A widow or widower in a same-sex marriage could be treated as a legal stranger for purposes of Social Security.

- **Medicaid and public benefits:** DOMA complicated how Massachusetts administered Medicaid and other joint federal-state programs. The state argued that it was forced to treat same-sex spouses differently from other married couples, potentially affecting eligibility rules, income calculations, and protections for spouses.

- **Veterans’ burial rights:** Same-sex spouses of veterans could be denied burial together in veterans’ cemeteries or access to related spousal honors and benefits. Massachusetts argued that DOMA interfered with the state’s operation of veterans’ cemeteries by preventing equal treatment of married same-sex couples.

Coakley’s case was one of the major legal challenges to DOMA. A federal judge later ruled in favor of Massachusetts, finding that the federal government had overstepped by refusing to recognize marriages valid under state law. The case helped build momentum toward the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2013 decision in **United States v. Windsor**, which struck down DOMA’s federal definition of marriage as unconstitutional.

**BOSTON —** Massachusetts is challenging the federal Defense of Marriage Act, arguing that the law unconstitutionally intrudes on the state’s authority to define marriage and forces Massachusetts to treat legally married same-sex couples as second-class citizens.

In a lawsuit filed in federal court, Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley said the 1996 law known as DOMA compels the state to deny equal treatment to same-sex spouses in programs that involve federal funding or federal rules, even though Massachusetts has recognized same-sex marriage since 2004.

Because of that definition, the federal government refuses to recognize same-sex marriages that are valid under state law. The result, Massachusetts argues, is a conflict between state and federal law: the state considers same-sex spouses legally married, while the federal government treats them as unmarried.

Massachusetts says that conflict has practical consequences across a wide range of state-administered programs. The complaint argues that DOMA affects areas such as Medicaid, tax administration, health benefits, and veterans’ services. In one example cited by state officials, federal rules tied to DOMA could jeopardize federal funding for state veterans’ cemeteries if Massachusetts allowed a same-sex spouse to be buried with a veteran on the same terms as an opposite-sex spouse.

The lawsuit names several federal agencies and officials, including the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, as defendants. Massachusetts contends that DOMA violates the **Tenth Amendment** by overriding the state’s traditional authority over marriage, and that it improperly requires the state to discriminate against its own citizens in order to receive or administer federal benefits.

Marriage law has historically been governed by the states, and Massachusetts argues that DOMA departs from that tradition. The state says the federal government has long relied on state determinations of marital status when administering federal programs, but DOMA creates a special exception for same-sex couples.

Supporters of DOMA have argued that Congress had authority to create a uniform federal definition of marriage and to protect states from being required to recognize same-sex marriages performed elsewhere. The law was enacted in 1996, before any state permitted same-sex couples to marry, and was signed by President Bill Clinton. It includes two major provisions: one allowing states to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages from other states, and another denying federal recognition to such marriages.

Massachusetts’ challenge focuses on the federal recognition provision.

Massachusetts became the first state to allow gay and lesbian couples to marry after the state Supreme Judicial Court ruled in *Goodridge v. Department of Public Health* that excluding same-sex couples from marriage violated the state constitution. Since then, several other states have moved toward recognition.

Vermont approved same-sex marriage legislatively, and New Hampshire also enacted a law to permit it. Maine’s legislature approved same-sex marriage as well, though the issue faced a public referendum. California briefly allowed same-sex marriages in 2008 before voters approved Proposition 8, halting new marriages while leaving thousands of existing marriages in legal limbo.

The Massachusetts lawsuit also arrived alongside separate legal challenges brought by gay-rights advocates on behalf of married same-sex couples denied federal benefits. Those plaintiffs argued that DOMA violates equal protection principles by denying federal recognition to marriages that are valid under state law.

For Massachusetts, however, the central argument is not only about individual rights but also about state power. The Commonwealth says it has made a lawful decision to recognize same-sex marriages and that the federal government may not penalize or undermine that decision by imposing a conflicting definition.

State officials said DOMA places Massachusetts in an untenable position: either disregard its own marriage laws and treat same-sex spouses unequally, or risk losing federal money and violating federal requirements.

“This is about equal treatment of our residents and respect for the decisions of the Commonwealth,” Coakley said. “The federal government should not be forcing Massachusetts to discriminate against married couples whom we have chosen to recognize.”

The case is expected to become part of a broader national battle over whether the federal government must recognize same-sex marriages legally performed in the states.
